prize_parts.citation: for incorporating firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory, changing how exporting, reallocation across firms and the gains from trade are analysed

statement.case_for: My configuration has changed: I now prefer B021 over B002. In round 1 I asked colleagues which later empirical work supports the collateral-feedback amplification claim in B002, and the exchange did not answer it. Hassler, Krusell, Teorell and Strömberg all describe the identification as mixed and as resting on calibrated models or later work by others. The chair's questions ask the same thing and the files do not resolve it. I cannot verify the answer from the permitted evidence, so I should not put a mechanism first when I cannot say whether its central claim has survived scrutiny. My other reason is practical, and I do not count it as merit: I doubted that B002 could reach six votes. B021 meets my own standard better. Melitz (2003) and the Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple work on exporting versus FDI make predictions about who exports, selection and reallocation. Those predictions have been confronted with firm-level data in many countries for over twenty years, according to the supporters' statements. I have not verified that evidence independently. The framework moved trade analysis from industries to firms and is the standard starting point for later quantitative work. The two-name attribution is among the cleanest on the shortlist. A citation worded around the selection model, not around all firm-level trade research, keeps the claim narrow and defensible. I also find Boppart's argument persuasive that firm selection is a new margin, not a refinement of the industry-level increasing-returns work recognised in 2008. B001 remains my first alternative. Krusell's separable-roles argument lowered my attribution concern, and the shortlist shows Calvo, Taylor and Woodford in ten of eleven opening proposals. I still rank B001 below B021 for my own reason, which is the empirical limit on the Calvo device that Friberg describes.
statement.case_against: The main reservation is credit. Bernard and Jensen (the firm-level exporter facts) and Eaton and Kortum (a parallel structural route to gains from trade) are outside this entry. A Helpman-Melitz prize could be read as rewarding the theory that organised facts documented by others. The welfare conclusions depend on functional-form assumptions such as Pareto productivity, so the citation should not rest on a particular size of the gains from trade. Melitz's contribution is concentrated in one seminal paper, though I do not treat that as disqualifying if the paper reorganised the field. Krugman's 2008 prize makes some members see this as the same lineage, and I cannot settle that from the evidence supplied. I also cannot confirm that quantitative trade models build on the heterogeneous-firm structure rather than supersede it, which Krusell raised. B001 has wider influence on policy practice and broader convergence on its three names. A committee that weights breadth of impact above credibility of evidence could reasonably choose it over B021.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B021 first. He treats Melitz (2003) as the central contribution, with Helpman's work on exporting versus FDI completing the core and Redding as derivative. He argues that firm selection is a distinct step from the new trade theory of 2008, and that quantitative trade models build on the heterogeneous-firm structure and do not replace it.
responses.response: This is the argument that moved me most. The distinction between industry-level increasing returns and firm-level selection is a difference in what is measured and tested, not only in the model, and that bears on my concern about credible evidence. I cannot verify the claim that the selection margin survives inside quantitative models, so I hold it provisionally. I also take his point that the credit boundary is a judgement. I agree the citation should name the selection model and not claim the Bernard-Jensen facts or the Eaton-Kortum route. My move to B021 is not a verdict on his conflict disclosures, which I treat as disclosed and not adjudicated.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B001 first and B021 third. He calls Helpman a natural co-recipient but says Melitz's contribution is largely one paper, that quantitative trade models may have absorbed part of the framework, and that B021 follows Krugman's 2008 prize. He says B001's trio separates into pricing device, contracts and rule, and microfounded synthesis.
responses.response: His separable-roles argument is why I no longer call B001 diffuse. Where I differ is that separable origin points do not settle whether the originating device matches the evidence. Friberg's own micro data show state-dependent adjustment that the Calvo device does not capture. I accept that a prize recognises influential benchmarks and not literal descriptions, and I list B001 as my first alternative for that reason. On single-paper concentration, I would not penalise it if later tests confirmed its predictions. On supersession, the question is whether the selection margin remains inside the newer models. He and Boppart disagree on this and I cannot resolve it from the supplied evidence, so I list it as an uncertainty.

responses.point: Hassler, the chair, ranks B002 first alongside me. He acknowledges that direct identification of collateral channels is mixed and comes mostly from later work by others. He ranked B021 sixth because of the overlap with Krugman's prize.
responses.response: I share his reasons for rating Kiyotaki-Moore highly: the mechanism is foundational, tractable and cleanly attributed. My own test was whether the collateral-feedback claim has survived scrutiny. Neither of us has shown that it has, and the chair's question 3 asks for exactly this evidence. I therefore cannot keep it as my preferred part without supporting evidence I have not seen. I keep it as an alternative because the attribution is clean and the mechanism is distinct from the 2022 banking work. On the Krugman overlap, I read Boppart's industry-versus-firm distinction as a real change in the unit of analysis. I do not think the overlap should lower B021 below B002, though I can see how a member might weigh it differently.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B021 first. He values that the framework connects theory to firm-level data and meets the standard of credible evidence he applies to empirical fields. He accepts the two-name core and says Redding is a successor. He flags credit for Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum and notes Helpman's separate B044 candidacy.
responses.response: I agree with his framing, and it is close to the reason for my move. I also agree that the committee should credit the selection model that organised the facts and not all firm-level trade research. The Helpman splitting risk is real. The B021 entry credits Helpman for firm-level work with Melitz and Yeaple, so the credit is separable. I would accept a citation worded to make this boundary explicit. We should not read the fact that two members now prefer B021 as evidence for it. My reasons are the testability of the selection predictions and the clean two-name attribution.

responses.point: Friberg prefers B001 with Taylor, Woodford and Calvo. He grants that micro evidence on price adjustment shows state dependence, so Calvo's device is a tractable approximation, but he treats this as a limit on the claim and not a refutation. He names B021 as a fallback if B001 stalls on attribution.
responses.response: His candour on the Calvo device is useful, and I accept his distinction between a limit on a claim and a refutation. We still weigh the limit differently. I give more weight to whether the central empirical prediction has been tested, and the selection predictions in B021 have been, by his own and Boppart's account. I also agree that B021 needs a citation built around the theory of selection and gains from trade, because the empirical pioneers are not on the entry. I welcome his fallback to B021 but I do not count it as support. My preference rests on my own reading of the evidence, and it differs from his on B001.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats the Helpman-Melitz selection model as a distinct step from the 2008 trade prize or as the same lineage.
Whether the selection margin survives inside newer quantitative trade models (Boppart's view) or has been partly superseded (Krusell's concern). I cannot resolve this from the supplied evidence.
Whether omitting Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum makes the credit incomplete even with a narrowly worded citation.
How sensitive the welfare and gains-from-trade results are to Pareto and other functional-form assumptions, which bears on how much of the citation can rest on gains from trade.
Whether later empirical work supports the B002 collateral-feedback claim. If a colleague showed that it does, B002's clean attribution would move it back up for me.
My assessments rest on general knowledge and the supplied files. I have not independently verified firm-level tests, citations or priority claims.
statement.conflict_note: No documented collaboration, institutional tie or personal connection to Helpman or Melitz in my supplied profile, nor to Kiyotaki, Moore, Calvo, Taylor or Woodford. My field of behavioural economics and metascience is adjacent to B004, which I do not prefer and whose credited names I have no tie to. Within the committee I have a long co-authorship with Magnus Johannesson, who is a former member and not a candidate. Other members' disclosed co-authorships (for example Friberg with the chair, and Boppart's field proximity to B021) are recorded and I do not adjudicate them. I have not verified any connection beyond what the profile states.
